claim: KServe and llm-d divide responsibilities cleanly: KServe handles model lifecycle/scaling/governance, LLMInferenceService supplies the generative API abstraction, vLLM executes inside the runtime, llm-d provides cross-runtime routing and cache awareness, and Kubernetes provides resource orchestration.
stance_target: llm-d's router role is architecturally scoped strictly to cross-instance scheduling, distinct from lifecycle/API/orchestration concerns -- which bounds what a non-k8s router replacement must reproduce
quoted_support: KServe acts as the control plane and LLMInferenceService delivers the generative API abstraction, while llm-d provides the cluster-wide optimization.

claim: llm-d benchmarks reported by the llm-d project (not independently reproduced by KServe) show up to ~57x faster P90 TTFT, throughput improving from ~4,400 to ~8,730 tokens/sec (~2x), sustained 4.5k-11k tokens/sec at scale, and ~50% P95/P99 tail latency reduction versus round-robin.
stance_target: KV-cache-aware routing materially outperforms naive round-robin load balancing at scale
scope_conditions: benchmarks published by the llm-d project, cited secondhand by KServe blog
quoted_support: Time to First Token (P90): Up to ~57× faster P90 TTFT in benchmark | Token Throughput: ~4,400 tokens/sec (baseline test cluster) -> ~8,730 tokens/sec (~2× improvement) | Tail Latency (P95/P99): ~50% tail latency reduction (reported tests)

claim: Naive round-robin load balancing for LLM serving produces five specific inefficiencies: cache locality loss, GPU imbalance, redundant prefill processing, high tail latency, and overprovisioned GPUs.
stance_target: round-robin/naive load balancing is adequate for LLM serving at scale
quoted_support: Naive Problems: Cache locality loss, GPU imbalance, Redundant prefill processing, High tail latency, Overprovisioned GPUs.
